title: The Make 'Em Proud Wall
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart shares an anecdote from a student, Abby V., who keeps photos of people she admires by her bedroom door and holds herself to a rule of not leaving her room unless she can promise not to disappoint them. He connects this to a mentor teacher's belief that everyone needs at least one person they cannot stand to disappoint, and to Tiger Woods's habit of imagining himself flanked by Arnold Palmer and Jack Nicklaus down the fairway. Stuart's point is that this whimsical teenage ritual is actually a serious motivational device — an external, personalized standard of character more vivid and more binding than an abstract value statement. He turned the idea into a writing prompt, having students name and write about who belongs on their own wall, and reports it became one of his favorite warm-ups of the year. The piece is offered as a shareable classroom activity rather than a research-backed strategy, in Stuart's typical practitioner-to-practitioner voice.
points: A personal 'wall' of people you refuse to disappoint functions as a concrete, emotionally sticky substitute for an abstract code of values.
The idea scales from an offhand student comment into a full class writing prompt with minimal setup — just ask students who's on their wall.
Elite performers use the same device deliberately: Tiger Woods imagined Arnold Palmer and Jack Nicklaus walking the fairway with him.
A mentor teacher's framing generalizes the technique beyond students to adults and colleagues: everyone needs someone they cannot stand to disappoint.
The prompt works partly because it's eclectic and personal rather than school-assigned, which is part of why it produced unusually engaged writing.
quotes: Last year, my student Abby V shared something that I found hilarious: in her bedroom, she has photos of people she looks up to hanging near her door, and she has a rule that applies to these people. Her rule for herself is that she is not allowed to leave her room unless she promises not to disappoint them.

When I shared this in a correspondence with my friend Jim, he said, "Diane McClain, one of my mentor teachers from Burlingame, just an amazing woman in her 70s now, said many times that we all need at least one person in our lives that we cannot stand the idea of disappointing.

And in his greater, much earlier days, Tiger Woods said he always imagined himself walking down the fairway every time with Arnold Palmer on one side and Jack Nicklaus on the other. It's a useful and demanding rubric of sorts.

The more I thought about it, the more I realized that Abby's wall wasn't just a funny thought — this spunky teenager walking out of her room, vowing not to disappoint the protagonist of Legally Blonde — but was in fact profound.
The responses were all over the place — some whimsical, some deep — and overall, it was probably my favorite writing warm-up prompt of the entire past school year.
